parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK technician: What are your main daily responsibilities, and what specific tasks do you need this new service to support?

My daily work involves keeping our drones and charging equipment in working order. I add new drones to our fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send them to charge. Regulators can ask us to show how our drones have been looked after.
ASK dispatcher: What are your main daily responsibilities, and what specific tasks do you need this new service to support?

As a dispatcher, I plan and run the flights for my company, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight. I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves or call it off. Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, so I need help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. My policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for me.
ASK desk: What are your main daily responsibilities, and what specific tasks do you need this new service to support?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. My desk works for all customer companies and has no business looking into any one company's operations.
ASK technician: What attributes and details do you need to record when adding, modifying, or retiring a drone?
ASK technician: What information must be tracked when a drone is taken out of service, repaired, or returned to service, and what must be kept for regulator records?
ASK technician: How do you manage charging pads at sites and what does the service need to do when you send a drone to charge?
Each of our company's sites has a few dozen of our own charging pads, and we never lend them to another company. We set up these charging pads at our sites, and we send drones to charge.
